title: Liguria - Coastal Wines
quiz.0.question: Which is Liguria’s most representative white grape?
quiz.0.explanation: Vermentino makes up more than 20% of Liguria’s plantings, making it the most widely planted grape, with aromatic herbs, elderflower, pear and a mineral-salty finish.
quiz.1.question: What is the main white grape of Cinque Terre?
quiz.1.explanation: Cinque Terre DOC makes only white wine, with at least 40% Bosco and up to 40% Albarola and/or Vermentino; Bosco gives structure.
quiz.2.question: What kind of wine is Sciacchetrà?
quiz.2.explanation: Sciacchetrà is Cinque Terre’s sweet white passito: the grapes are gradually dried on well-ventilated racks, minimum alcohol is 13.5%, and it cannot be released before November of the following year.
quiz.3.question: What is the defining feature of Liguria’s vineyards?
quiz.3.explanation: Liguria has no flat land for vines; vineyards lie on steep coastal terraces or inland slopes, which is why its viticulture is called “heroic”.
slides.0.title: 🌊 Liguria
slides.0.subtitle: Steep vineyards under the Mediterranean sun
slides.1.title: 🏛️ History and Cultural Heritage
slides.1.content:
Ligurian wine has a long history: from Roman times to the maritime trade of the Republic of Genoa, it shaped the region’s distinctive wine culture.

🏺

Pre-Roman and Roman times

The Liguri tribe settled here well before 1000 BC and planted vines on the steep slopes before formal viticulture was introduced by the Greeks and Etruscans. By the Roman era the wines of the Cinque Terre coast were renowned, and those of the Roman town of Luni were so esteemed that Pliny the Elder mentioned them in his Naturalis Historia. The steep terraced vineyards date back to Roman times.

⚓

The Republic of Genoa

In the Middle Ages Genoa, Liguria’s main port, was a powerful city-state; as the Maritime Republic of Genoa it expanded over the surrounding territory and became one of the major military and commercial powers of the Mediterranean.

🏛️

14th century: the wine trade

The wine trade became a significant source of income for the Republic, and vines covered two-thirds of Liguria’s cultivated land. Genoa even created a government body to protect and support wine consumption, as a way to protect people from disease, epidemics and unsafe drinking water.

📉

17th century: peak and decline

Viticulture peaked in the 17th century and then faltered: political instability and British and Dutch competition at sea undermined Genoa’s commercial power, and many growers abandoned their vines and planted olives instead.

⚔️

Napoléon and Italian unification

Instability continued into the 19th century, when the Republic briefly became part of Napoléon’s French Empire. After the Napoleonic Wars the Congress of Vienna gave the Republic’s territory to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which went on to unite most of the peninsula as the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

🦠

Late 19th century: phylloxera

Phylloxera all but destroyed the industry. The steep terraces were costly to maintain and offered little return, so many were abandoned; winegrowing only rebounded in the 1960s-1970s alongside the growing tourist trade.

🏔️

1972

Rossese di Dolceacqua became the first Ligurian wine to gain DOC status.

🏆

National Park and World Heritage

Cinque Terre is a National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

🌊

21st century: a turn to quality

Producers once favoured quantity to supply resorts and restaurants; in the 21st century many have embraced the region’s winegrowing heritage, and quality has risen, with wines of distinct regional individuality.

🌟 Liguria’s cultural standing

🇮🇹 The Italian Riviera

Its spectacular coast and fishing villages make Liguria an important tourist destination; tourism is the region’s main source of income.

🌍 World Heritage

The terraced vineyards of Cinque Terre are an iconic landscape of people living with steep terrain.

🍷 Drunk locally

Production is small and largely drunk by summer visitors, though the wines are increasingly noticed beyond the region.
slides.2.title: 🏖️ Italy’s “Riviera”
slides.2.content:
Liguria is a narrow, crescent-shaped strip of north-west Italy facing the Ligurian Sea — Italy’s third-smallest region — famous for the steep terraced vineyards of Cinque Terre. Production is small but full of character.

🏖️
350 kmof rocky coastline (220 miles)
⛰️
65% / 35%mountains / hills — no flat land
🍷
8DOCs (2017)

🏔️ Heroic viticulture

Vines can only be grown on steep coastal terraces or slightly gentler inland slopes, with no flat land available; such hard, labour-intensive conditions are why Ligurian viticulture is called “heroic”.
slides.3.title: 🗺️ Liguria DOC Interactive Map
slides.4.title: 🌍 Topography, Climate, Industry Data and More Grapes (IWS)
slides.4.content:
A crescent shaped by two mountain ranges

Liguria is shaped by two mountain ranges that almost merge with the coast: the Maritime Alps to the north-west and the Ligurian Apennines to the north-east. The region is 65% mountains and 35% hills, with no plains, and the mountains and hills often rise straight out of the sea. Four coastal cities give their names to the four provinces: Imperia, Savona, Genoa and La Spezia; Genoa is the capital and Italy’s major commercial port.

Two winegrowing sub-regions: Riviera di Ponente (the west coast, from the French border to Genoa, covering Savona and Imperia provinces; the largest and driest, with the widest range of meso-climates) · Riviera di Levante (the east coast, from east of Genoa to the Tuscan border, including Cinque Terre, La Spezia province and Portofino; small sandy capes and cliffs, with terraces held up by dry-stone walls)

Climate and soil data

Temperature: the average annual temperature is highest on the coast (57°F/14°C), dropping to 54°F/12°C inland; the mountains block cold northerly winds and the sea moderates diurnal swings
Rainfall: sea breezes bring humidity and rain falls mainly in autumn and winter. The eastern Riviera di Levante is wetter because of the prevailing southerly winds, with 67 in/1,700 mm a year; the western Riviera di Ponente is drier, with under 30 in/800 mm
Soils: generally poor and stony, in two main types — reddish calcareous marl in the western Ponente, and a mix of clay, sand and limestone in the eastern Levante
Training: the western Riviera traditionally uses alberello (bush vines); the eastern Riviera uses the overhead pergola, with a local low variant in Cinque Terre; because these are labour-intensive, vertical systems are becoming more common

Industry scale

Liguria has the second-smallest vineyard area in Italy after Valle d'Aosta, about 3,700 acres/1,500 ha; more than 40% of the vineyard land belongs to growers with under 2.5 acres/1 ha, often split into several plots. As of 2017 there are 8 DOCs; DOC wine is over 70% of production, IGT under 15% and generic wine under 15% — one of the highest DOC shares in Italy

Plantings and other grapes

Most widely planted grapes (ISTAT, 2010): Vermentino 23% · Pigato 12% · Rossese 10% · Albarola 5% · Ormeasco 5% · Sangiovese 5% · Bosco 4% · Others 36%
Rossese and France: DNA profiling has shown Rossese to be genetically identical to France’s Tibouren, though it cannot yet be said whether it originated in Italy or France; it has been grown in Liguria since at least the 1700s
Albarola = Bianchetta Genovese: DNA studies have proven them to be the same grape, mainly grown in the Golfo del Tigullio and Val Polcevera DOCs, though the National Registry and the DOC rules still list them separately
Sangiovese in Liguria: grown mainly in the eastern Riviera di Levante, it is the main component of the reds of Colli di Luni DOC and Colline di Levanto DOC
Other whites: Scimiscià, Trebbiano Toscano, Lumassina, Albana, Malvasia Bianca, Moscato Bianco, Rollo, Rossese Bianco, Ruzzese; other reds: Canaiolo Nero, Pollera Nera, Albarossa, Barbera (plus Vermentino Nero and Granaccia, introduced elsewhere)
slides.5.title: ⛰️ Heroic Viticulture
slides.5.content:
🏔️ “Heroic” viticulture

Ligurian viticulture is called heroic: vines can only be grown on steep coastal terraces or slightly gentler inland slopes, with no flat land, in extremely hard and labour-intensive conditions.

🌄 Terraced vineyards

65%

Mountains

The other 35% is hills, and mountains and hills often rise straight from the sea.

Roman

The terraces’ origin

The steep terraces date back to Roman times and must be reworked regularly to prevent erosion and landslides.

Dry-stone

Walls

In the Riviera di Levante the very steep, narrow terraces are held up by dry-stone walls overlooking the sea.

1,500 ha

Vineyard area

The second smallest in Italy after Valle d'Aosta.

🧱 Training systems
Western Riviera: traditionally alberello (bush vines)
Eastern Riviera: traditionally the overhead pergola
Cinque Terre: a local low variant of the pergola
Trend: because traditional systems are so labour-intensive, vertical training is becoming more common

👷 Hard work

🚫
No flat land

Vines grow only on steep terraces or inland slopes, and most of the work is done by hand.

🌊
Next to the waves

In Cinque Terre the vines are so close to the sea that they are misted by the spray of waves.

🚂
Monorails

At harvest, monorails carry crates of grapes from the vineyard to the nearest road.

💰
Little return

After phylloxera, many costly, low-return terraces were abandoned.

🔧 Vineyard challenges

🧱 Terrace upkeep

Terraces must be reworked regularly to prevent erosion and landslides.

🏚️ Abandoned vineyards

Many vineyards were abandoned over the centuries; only recently have quality-minded producers revived the most challenging sites.

☀️ Summer drought

Summers are warm and dry with the least rain, and drought can be an issue in very hot years.

👨‍🌾 Small holdings

More than 40% of the vineyard land belongs to growers with under 1 ha, often split into several plots.

💎 Why is it worth it?

🌊
Regional character

The wines show distinct regional individuality: refreshing, vibrant whites and distinctive reds.

🧂
A saline finish

Acidity is often combined with a saline note, perfect with local seafood.

🍇
Over 100 grapes

Liguria grows more than 100 varieties, mostly co-planted native grapes.

🏛️
Cultural heritage

A terraced landscape that has endured since Roman times.

📊 The two sub-regions compared

Riviera di Ponente (west)Riviera di Levante (east)
AreaFrench border to Genoa, Savona and Imperia provincesEast of Genoa to the Tuscan border
RainfallUnder 800 mm, the driestAbout 1,700 mm, wetter
SoilsReddish calcareous marlClay, sand and limestone
TrainingAlberelloPergola
WinesEntirely single-varietalVarietals plus red and white blends
SignaturesPigato, Vermentino, RosseseCinque Terre, Colli di Luni Vermentino
slides.6.title: 🍇 The Main White Grapes
slides.6.content:
Most planted

Vermentino

Share: over 20%, Liguria’s most planted grape

Flavours: aromatic herbs (fennel, sage, thyme), elderflower, pear

Hallmark: a distinctive mineral-salty finish

Where: varietal and blended; Colli di Luni Vermentino is one of the most distinctive wines

Western classic

Pigato

Where: the classic white of the western Riviera (Savona and Imperia provinces)

Flavours: lightly herbal, stone fruit, sage and honey, often musky

Hallmark: a saline finish; Riviera Ligure di Ponente Pigato needs at least 95%

Identity: research shows it is genetically identical to Vermentino, but it is registered separately

Backbone of Cinque Terre

Bosco

Identity: a hardy native from La Spezia

Where: mainly the eastern Riviera di Levante, often in vineyards right by the sea

Use: blended with Vermentino and Albarola into Cinque Terre DOC (at least 40%)

Role: adds body and structure to the blend
slides.7.title: 🍇 Vermentino and the Native Grapes in Depth
slides.7.content:
🌟 Vermentino in depth

🌍 Vermentino and Pigato

Genetically identical

DNA: recent research shows Vermentino and Pigato are genetically identical

Terroir: they have adapted differently to Ligurian conditions and make wines of distinct character

Rules: the National Registry and the DOC rules still list them separately

🔍 Pigato is the classic white of the western Riviera

Liguria’s synonyms
Pigato = Vermentino

Genetically identical, but treated as two grapes and registered separately.

Albarola = Bianchetta Genovese

DNA has proven them the same, but the registry and DOC rules still list them separately.

Ormeasco = Dolcetto

Ormeasco is the Ligurian name for Dolcetto.

🔬 Pigato vs Vermentino: one grape, two styles

VermentinoPigato

Share of plantings23% (the most)12%
Main areaThe whole regionSavona and Imperia in the west
AromasFennel, sage, thyme, elderflower, pearHerbs, stone fruit, sage, honey, musk
FinishMineral-saltySaline
Ponente DOC ruleAt least 95%At least 95%
Best sub-zoneColli di Luni (east)Albenganese (west)

Fruit

Pear

Floral

Elderflower

Herbal

Fennel, sage, thyme

A mineral-salty finish

Structure

Refreshing acidity

🌍 What shapes Ligurian whites

🌊 The sea: moderates and narrows the diurnal temperature swing
⛰️ The mountains: the Maritime Alps and Ligurian Apennines block cold northerly winds
🪨 Poor, stony soils: reddish calcareous marl in the west; clay, sand and limestone in the east
☀️ Summer: warm and dry, moderated by sea breezes

📍 The main Vermentino appellations

Colli di Luni DOC

Rule: at least 90% Vermentino

Where: the east, shared with Toscana

Character: similar to the Vermentino of north-west Toscana, and one of Liguria’s most distinctive wines

Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC

Rule: at least 95% Vermentino

Where: the west, Liguria’s largest DOC

Character: a classic varietal alongside Pigato and Rossese

🍷 Liguria’s other native grapes

Bosco

White

Identity: a hardy native from La Spezia

Where: the Riviera di Levante, often right by the sea

Rule: Cinque Terre DOC needs at least 40%

Role: gives the blend structure

Albarola

White

Identity: the same grape as Bianchetta Genovese

Where: mainly the Golfo del Tigullio and Val Polcevera DOCs

Role: provides acidity in the Cinque Terre blend

Share: about 5%

Rossese

Red

Identity: genetically identical to France’s Tibouren; its country of origin is unresolved

Where: almost entirely the western Riviera di Ponente, 10% of plantings there

History: grown since at least the 1700s; the most planted red grape

Style: pale ruby, medium body, bright acidity, floral, red berries, herbs, spice and a savoury note

Ormeasco

Red

Identity: the Ligurian name for Dolcetto

Where: Ormeasco di Pornassio DOC

Style: more herbal and lighter than Piemonte’s Dolcetto

Share: about 5%

Granaccia

Red

Identity: Cannonau (Grenache)

Where: Riviera Ligure di Ponente Granaccia

Sub-zone: Quiliano is dedicated to dry red Granaccia

Sangiovese

Red

Where: mainly the eastern Riviera di Levante

Use: the main component of the reds of Colli di Luni DOC and Colline di Levanto DOC

Share: about 5%

slides.8.title: 🏞️ Cinque Terre
slides.8.content:
🌈 World Heritage vineyards

Cinque Terre (“five lands”) refers to five fishing villages on the cliffs north of La Spezia: Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore. It is a National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Liguria’s most spectacular terraced vineyards.

⚪ Cinque Terre DOC

Grapes: at least 40% Bosco, up to 40% Albarola and/or Vermentino, up to 20% other white grapes

Style: refreshing acidity, light minerality, citrus and herbs

Body: light, moderate alcohol

Sub-zones: Costa de Sera, Costa de Campu, Costa da Posa

Note: white wine only

🍯 Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà

Type: sweet white passito from dried grapes

Grapes: the same Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino as Cinque Terre

Style: white flowers, dried apricot, dried figs, honey, almonds, spice, with a mineral core

Alcohol: at least 13.5%

Release: not before November of the following year; Riserva after three years

Note: made only in the best years, in tiny quantities

💡 Each grape has a role: Bosco gives structure, Vermentino adds perfume and Albarola provides acidity.
slides.9.title: 🍷 Label Example: Cinque Terre DOC
slides.9.caption: Cinque Terre DOC “Costa da Posa” Vendemmia 2019 — bottled by the cooperative of growers from the five villages of Riomaggiore, Manarola, Corniglia, Vernazza and Monterosso; the bottom of the label reads “Imbottigliato nella zona di produzione” (bottled in the production area).
slides.10.title: 🍯 Sciacchetrà in Depth
slides.10.content:
💎 The treasure of Cinque Terre

Sciacchetrà is made only in the best years and is highly sought after for its tiny production — a resuscitated gem, rightly considered among the best of all Italian passitos.

📜 Getting to know Sciacchetrà

📖
Where

Within Cinque Terre DOC, the narrow coastal strip from Monterosso to La Spezia.

🍇
Grapes

The same blend as Cinque Terre: at least 40% Bosco, plus Albarola and/or Vermentino.

💰
Rarity

Made only in the best years, in tiny quantities.

⚠️
Don’t confuse

The rosato of Ormeasco di Pornassio is called Sciac-trà — a completely different wine.

🍇 How it is made

Stage 1: harvest

Picked on the steep terraces, with monorails carrying crates of grapes to the nearest road.

Stage 2: drying

The grapes are gradually dehydrated on well-ventilated racks in well-ventilated rooms.

Stage 3: fermentation

The must is fermented in chestnut barrels or stainless steel, reaching at least 13.5% alcohol.

Stage 4: release

Not before November of the following year; Riserva only after three years.

🎨 Two categories

TypeReleaseAppearanceMain flavoursAlcoholAppellation
SciacchetràFrom November of the following yearGolden-amberWhite flowers, dried apricot, dried figs, honeyAt least 13.5%Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà DOC
RiservaAfter three yearsGolden-amberAlmonds, spice, a mineral coreAt least 13.5%As above

🆚 Compared with other Italian sweet wines

vs Vin Santo (Toscana)

✓ Both are sweet wines from dried grapes

✓ Sciacchetrà is a Bosco blend from coastal terraces

vs Vino Santo (Trentino)

✓ Trentino’s Vino Santo is made from Nosiola

✓ Similar names, completely different wines

vs Picolit (Friuli)

✓ Picolit is a single-varietal sweet wine

✓ Sciacchetrà is a three-grape blend

What makes it unique

Grapes grown on terraces misted by the waves give a mineral core.

🍽️ Food and serving

🍰 Classic pairings
  • Pandolce - Genoa’s traditional sweet bread
  • Cantucci - almond biscuits
  • Blue cheese - sweet and salty contrast
  • Apricot tart - echoes the dried apricot
  • Aged hard cheeses
  • Nut desserts
🍷 Serving tips

Temperature: lightly chilled

Glass: a small dessert-wine or white-wine glass

Pour: small glasses, sipped slowly

Occasion: with dessert, for meditation, for celebrations
slides.11.title: 🌊 The Influence of the Sea
slides.11.content:
🌊

Moderated by the sea

The sea moderates and narrows the diurnal swing; the coast averages about 14°C a year, inland 12°C.

🧂

A saline finish

Ligurian wines often pair acidity with a saline note, ideal for local seafood.

⛰️

Mountain barrier

The Maritime Alps and Ligurian Apennines block cold northerly winds.

🌡️

Mediterranean climate

Broadly Mediterranean, with some continental influence in the inland valleys.
slides.12.title: 🌊 Climate, Soils and Seasons
slides.12.content:
🌤️ Climate data (IWS)

14°C

Average annual temperature on the coast (12°C inland)

1,700 mm

Annual rainfall in the eastern Levante

<800 mm

Annual rainfall in the western Ponente

Autumn-winter

When most rain falls

🌊 What shapes the climate

🌬️
Sea breezes and southerly winds

Sea breezes: bring humidity; rain is plentiful but falls mainly in autumn and winter.

Southerly winds: the prevailing southerlies make the eastern Riviera di Levante wetter than the west.

Result: it gets drier from east to west, with the western Ponente the driest.

⛰️
The mountains

North-west: the Maritime Alps

North-east: the Ligurian Apennines

Effect: running almost into the coast, they protect the region from cold northerly winds.

🌊
The sea

Effect: moderates and narrows the diurnal swing.

Summer: warm and dry, moderated by sea breezes; the least rain, with drought possible in very hot years.

Winter: mild on the coast, colder in the inland valleys, with significant rain.

🪨 The two main soil types

Western Ponente

Soils: reddish calcareous marl

Character: poor and stony

Appellations: Riviera Ligure di Ponente, Rossese di Dolceacqua (red calcareous soil)

Eastern Levante

Soils: a mix of clay, sand and limestone

Character: poor and stony

Appellations: Cinque Terre, Colli di Luni

Overall

Character: poor and stony

Landscape: 65% mountains, 35% hills

Coast: 350 km of rocky shoreline

📅 Liguria through the seasons

🌸 Spring and summer

Spring: mild with little rain.

Summer: warm and dry, moderated by sea breezes; the least rain, with drought possible in very hot years.

🍂 Autumn and winter

Autumn: mild temperatures and the most rain.

Winter: mild on the coast, colder in the inland valleys, with significant rain.

🆚 West vs east

FeatureRiviera di Ponente (west)Riviera di Levante (east)
RainfallUnder 800 mmAbout 1,700 mm
SizeThe largestSmaller
Meso-climatesThe most diverseCoastal cliffs and sandy capes
SoilsReddish calcareous marlClay, sand, limestone
GrapesPigato, Vermentino, Rossese, OrmeascoBosco, Albarola, Vermentino, Sangiovese
StyleEntirely single-varietalVarietals and blends

🧂 The style of Ligurian wine

1. Mostly white

White wines are over half of production, defined by crisp acidity and a mineral-saline character.

2. Light reds

Reds tend to be light and refreshing, often with a distinctive herbal-earthy note.

3. Mostly white grapes

Over 70% are white varieties; international grapes are a tiny share, mostly for IGT.

4. Blending rules

The DOCs set minimum proportions of the main local grapes in blends and varietals; the balance can be any authorised grape.

🍽️ In short: acidity combined with a saline note makes Ligurian wine the perfect match for local seafood and regional dishes.
slides.13.title: 🗺️ The Appellations of the Riviera di Ponente (IWS)
slides.13.content:
Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC — Liguria’s largest DOC

This DOC covers most of western Liguria, from San Remo to the west side of Genoa, and is Liguria’s largest DOC by vineyard area. It makes classic varietal whites from Pigato and Vermentino and reds from Rossese.

The main wines: Pigato (at least 95%) · Vermentino (at least 95%) · Moscato (Moscato Bianco, dry and passito) · Rossese (at least 90%, also passito) · plus a red from Granaccia (Cannonau)

Five variety-specific sub-zones

Albenganese, Finalese, Riviera dei Fiori: sub-zones for Pigato, Vermentino and Rossese; Albenganese is known for some of the best Pigatos, and Finalese for some of the most distinctive wines in Liguria
Taggia: a sub-zone for sweet Moscato Bianco
Quiliano: a sub-zone for dry red Granaccia

Val Polcevera DOC — Liguria’s smallest DOC

The coastal hills west of Genoa and the inland hills along the Polcevera river. It makes refreshing whites from Vermentino and Bianchetta Genovese (i.e. Albarola), blended or varietal, and a red from Dolcetto, Ciliegiolo and Sangiovese. The Coronata sub-zone around Genoa is limited to white blends

Rossese di Dolceacqua DOC — Liguria’s first DOC (1972)

History: the wines of Dolceacqua have been admired since at least the 19th century, even by Napoléon; in 1972 it became the first Ligurian wine to gain DOC status
Terroir: around the medieval town of Dolceacqua by the French border, at 990-2,000 ft/300-600 m, on terraced, rocky slopes of red calcareous soil that retain water and are buffeted by winds
Rules: at least 95% Rossese; superiore must age at least 1 year and reach at least 13% abv; 38 MGAs (additional geographic designations) can follow the DOC name, the best known including Arcagna, Luvaira, Pini, Curli, Posaù and Galeae
Style: good tannic structure, medium body, red fruit and spice, suited to medium-term ageing; more intense, deeper and spicier than Rossese Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC

Ormeasco di Pornassio DOC

Entirely in the mountainous inland area north-west of Imperia, with vineyards up to 2,600 ft/800 m. Wines are made from at least 95% Ormeasco (the local name for Dolcetto) and are floral, fruity and spicy with a slightly bitter finish; the classic style is dry, and superiore needs higher minimum alcohol and at least 1 year of ageing
⚠️ Don’t confuse the two: Ormeasco di Pornassio can also be made as a fruity, short skin-contact rosato labelled Sciac-trà, or as a sweet red passito from dried grapes — completely different from Cinque Terre’s sweet white Sciacchetrà
slides.14.title: 🗺️ The Appellations of the Riviera di Levante (IWS)
slides.14.content:
The blending rules of Cinque Terre DOC

This DOC covers the narrow coastal strip from Monterosso to La Spezia and makes white wine only. The blend: at least 40% Bosco, up to 40% Albarola and/or Vermentino, and up to 20% other authorised white grapes. Each grape plays a role — Bosco gives structure, Vermentino adds perfume and Albarola provides acidity.

Three official sub-zones (which may follow the DOC name, with slightly stricter maximum yields and alcohol): Costa de Sera · Costa de Campu · Costa da Posa

Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà — the rules

The grapes are gradually dried on well-ventilated racks in well-ventilated rooms, and the must is fermented in chestnut barrels or stainless steel. The wine must reach at least 13.5% abv and cannot be released before November of the following year; Riserva can only be released after three years. It is golden-amber, with white flowers, dried apricot, dried figs, honey, almonds and spice around a mineral core

Colli di Luni DOC — shared with Toscana

It covers most of the eastern Riviera di Levante plus three towns in north-west Toscana, and takes its name from the hills (colli) around the ancient Roman town of Luni. The Tuscan influence shows in the grapes: reds are based on Sangiovese, and the white blends include Trebbiano Toscano
Four official wines: Colli di Luni Vermentino (at least 90% Vermentino) · Colli di Luni Albarola (at least 85% Albarola) · Colli di Luni Rosso (Sangiovese-based) · Colli di Luni Bianco (Vermentino and Trebbiano Toscano); the Vermentino here resembles that of north-west Toscana and is one of Liguria’s most distinctive wines

Colline di Levanto DOC and Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino DOC

Colline di Levanto DOC: a small DOC around the town of Levanto, between the Golfo del Tigullio and Cinque Terre DOCs, making light, fresh, simple whites from Vermentino, Albarola and Bosco, and a red from Vermentino, Sangiovese and Ciliegiolo
Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino DOC: the coastal and inland hills from the east side of Genoa to Deiva Marina. Whites are made from Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese, Sciascia and Moscato Bianco; reds from Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese, Ciliegiolo and Dolcetto

slides.16.title: 🍴 Ligurian Food Culture
slides.16.content:
🌿 The home of pesto

Pesto alla Genovese was born in Liguria and is one of the world’s most famous Italian sauces.

🌿 Pasta with pesto

Wine: Vermentino (its herbal notes echo the basil)

🐟 Ligurian fish soup

Wine: Cinque Terre DOC (saline minerality to match)

🥖 Focaccia

Wine: Pigato (pairs with the olive oil)

🐟 Fried anchovies

Wine: Vermentino (high acidity cuts the oil)

🍰 Sciacchetrà

Food: Cantucci biscuits, pandolce sweet bread
slides.17.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.17.points.0: ✓ Liguria is known for its steep coastal terraces; it has Italy’s second-smallest vineyard area (after Valle d’Aosta), and over 70% of its production is DOC
slides.17.points.1: ✓ There are 8 DOCs, in the western Riviera di Ponente (Riviera Ligure di Ponente, Val Polcevera, Rossese di Dolceacqua, Ormeasco di Pornassio) and the eastern Riviera di Levante (Cinque Terre, Colli di Luni, Colline di Levanto, Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino)
slides.17.points.2: ✓ Rossese di Dolceacqua was Liguria’s first DOC (1972); do not confuse Sciac-trà (an Ormeasco rosato) with Cinque Terre’s sweet Sciacchetrà
slides.17.points.3: ✓ Vermentino shows a distinctive maritime minerality and saline character
slides.17.points.4: ✓ Vermentino (23%) and Pigato (12%) are genetically identical but registered separately; Rossese (= Tibouren) is the most planted red
slides.17.points.5: ✓ Cinque Terre DOC is white only, with at least 40% Bosco; Cinque Terre is a National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
slides.17.points.6: ✓ Sciacchetrà is a sweet white from dried grapes, min. 13.5% ABV, not released before November of the following year; Riserva after three years
slides.17.points.7: ✓ The western Ponente is drier (under 800 mm) with reddish calcareous marl; the eastern Levante is wetter (about 1,700 mm)
slides.18.title: 🧠 Liguria Knowledge Check
slides.18.questions.0.question: Which is Liguria’s most representative white grape?
slides.18.questions.0.explanation: Vermentino makes up more than 20% of Liguria’s plantings, making it the most widely planted grape, with aromatic herbs, elderflower, pear and a mineral-salty finish.
slides.18.questions.1.question: What is the main white grape of Cinque Terre?
slides.18.questions.1.explanation: Cinque Terre DOC makes only white wine, with at least 40% Bosco and up to 40% Albarola and/or Vermentino; Bosco gives structure.
slides.18.questions.2.question: What kind of wine is Sciacchetrà?
slides.18.questions.2.explanation: Sciacchetrà is Cinque Terre’s sweet white passito: the grapes are gradually dried on well-ventilated racks, minimum alcohol is 13.5%, and it cannot be released before November of the following year.
slides.18.questions.3.question: What is the defining feature of Liguria’s vineyards?
slides.18.questions.3.explanation: Liguria has no flat land for vines; vineyards lie on steep coastal terraces or inland slopes, which is why its viticulture is called “heroic”.
slides.18.questions.4.question: Which food suits Ligurian Vermentino best?
slides.18.questions.4.explanation: Ligurian wines often combine acidity with a saline note, making them a perfect match for local seafood and regional specialities.
slides.18.questions.5.question: Which was the first Ligurian wine to gain DOC status?
slides.18.questions.5.explanation: Rossese di Dolceacqua became Liguria’s first DOC in 1972; even Napoléon expressed his admiration for it.
slides.18.questions.6.question: DNA research has shown Rossese to be identical to which grape?
slides.18.questions.6.explanation: Rossese is genetically identical to France’s Tibouren, but it is still not certain whether it originated in Italy or France.
slides.18.questions.7.question: Ormeasco is the Ligurian name for which grape?
slides.18.questions.7.explanation: Ormeasco is the local name for Dolcetto, used in Ormeasco di Pornassio DOC; it is more herbal and lighter than Piemonte’s Dolcetto.
slides.18.questions.8.question: Which region shares the Colli di Luni DOC with Liguria?
slides.18.questions.8.explanation: Colli di Luni is an inter-regional DOC shared by Liguria and Toscana; its reds are Sangiovese-based and its Vermentino needs at least 90%.
slides.18.questions.9.question: What is “Sciac-trà”?
slides.18.questions.9.options.1: B. The rosato of Ormeasco di Pornassio
slides.18.questions.9.explanation: Sciac-trà is the fruity, short skin-contact rosato of Ormeasco di Pornassio; do not confuse it with Sciacchetrà, the sweet white of Cinque Terre.
